introduction: These readings ask for two things at once: that the outward meaning of the sacred text be kept, and that its inner meaning be sought. Whoever takes one and abandons the other is called ignorant or heedless. They go on to read the Gospel's supper, resurrection, falling stars and throne of David as figures, and to speak of names, lamps and appearances that hide what they carry. Each of the ninety-one quotations is read here beside one from elsewhere. Most stand alongside: the Talmud, Augustine, Aquinas and the Qur'an on plain and further senses, the Gospels on parables, Paul on letter and spirit, Origen, Maimonides, Rumi, Kabir, Shakespeare and Emerson. Some push back: Aquinas allows argument only from the literal sense, Paul stakes everything on a risen Christ, Luke and Acts tell the stories plainly, and Hume doubts that the books agree.
questions: The first reading calls the one who keeps both the outward and the inward meaning a perfect sage. Which of the two do you more easily let go, and what is lost when you do?

Some readings close the gates of interpretation and hold to the plain meaning; others say that the words of the prophets were all allegories. How do the readings fit these together, and where does Aquinas's rule help or hinder?
Paul says that if Christ be not risen, faith is vain; the readings speak of a resurrection that is not of the body. What is each protecting?
The disciples misunderstood 'Lazarus sleepeth' and 'destroy this temple'. How can a reader tell when a text is speaking in figures?
The readings say that until one passes beyond the river of names one does not reach the ocean of meanings. What names have stood between you and a meaning?
Several readings and several quotations here speak of people whose outside and inside differ. What would it look like for the outer to be identical with the inner?

outside.why: The Talmud holds that a verse does not depart from its literal meaning, although there may be additional interpretations.
Augustine, when one reader says the author meant this and another that, asks: why not rather as both, if both be true?
Mark says that Jesus spoke to the people only in parables, and expounded all things to his disciples when they were alone.
The letter to the Hebrews calls the word of God quick and powerful, piercing to the dividing of soul and spirit.
Paul prays that the whole spirit and soul and body of his readers be preserved blameless.
Peter's letter says that no prophecy of the scripture is of any private interpretation.
The Qur'an distinguishes clear revelations, the substance of the Book, from others which are allegorical.
Emerson says that every scripture is to be interpreted by the same spirit which gave it forth. If the gates of interpretation are closed, what is left for the reader's own spirit to do?
Paul tells the Corinthians that he fed them with milk and not with meat, for they were not yet able to bear it.
Proverbs sets as the aim of learning to understand a proverb and the interpretation, the words of the wise and their dark sayings.
Joseph asks the prisoners who have dreamed: do not interpretations belong to God?
The Qur'an says that all kinds of similitudes have been coined in it for mankind, that they may reflect.
Paul speaks of a vail that remains upon the heart in the reading of the scripture.
Jeremiah foresees a law put in the inward parts and written in the hearts.
Rumi opens his poem with a reed-flute that complains of its banishment from its home, and means more than a reed.
Aristotle held that the greatest thing by far is to have a command of metaphor.
The Tao Teh King opens by saying that the name that can be named is not the enduring and unchanging name.
Pascal says that the heart has its reasons, which reason does not know.
Luke says of the risen Jesus that he opened their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures.
Maimonides read Isaiah's wolf dwelling with the lamb as a metaphor and a parable.
Aquinas held that all the senses of scripture are founded on the literal, from which alone can any argument be drawn. If every prophecy is an allegory, what can be argued from it, and by whom?
At the supper Jesus took bread and said: take, eat; this is my body. Christians have divided for centuries over how these words are meant. What makes one reading of them more than a preference?
In John's Gospel Jesus says, after speaking of bread from heaven, that it is the spirit that quickeneth and the flesh profiteth nothing.
These are the words that many of his hearers could not bear: except ye eat the flesh of the Son of man, ye have no life in you.
Jesus says of John the Baptist: if ye will receive it, this is Elias, which was for to come.

In Acts two men in white tell the disciples that Jesus shall so come in like manner as they have seen him go into heaven. How does the reading's argument meet those who take that promise as it stands?
This is the saying the reading quotes: the Son of man which is in heaven, said by one standing on earth.
Jesus says, destroy this temple and in three days I will raise it up; his hearers think of the building, and he spake of his body.
Paul writes that if Christ be not risen, then is our preaching vain, and your faith is also vain. Does a resurrection of teachings and influence carry the weight Paul lays on it?

Luke's account has the disciples terrified, supposing that they had seen a spirit, and Jesus standing in the midst of them. What does the story lose and keep when the fish and honeycomb are read as symbols?
When Jesus says that Lazarus sleepeth, the disciples take him at his word, and the Gospel explains that he spake of his death. How is a reader to tell when the text itself is speaking in figures?
Paul already reads the passage through the sea spiritually: they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them.

This is the account in Exodus: the waters were divided and the people went through on dry ground. What would a spiritual reading have to keep of the story for it to remain the story of a people's deliverance?
Origen asked who that has understanding will suppose that the first three days, evening and morning, existed without a sun.
This is the saying in question: the sun shall be darkened, and the stars shall fall from heaven.
John's vision speaks of a new heaven and a new earth, the first heaven and the first earth having passed away.
The same book shows a woman clothed with the sun, the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head.
Paul reads Abraham's two sons as an allegory, and speaks of a Jerusalem which is above and is free.
John sees the holy city, new Jerusalem, coming down from God out of heaven.
This is the language of the Song of Solomon: my beloved is mine, and I am his.
Paul puts it in a sentence that became a proverb: the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.
Jesus says that he has spoken in proverbs, but the time cometh when he shall show them plainly of the Father.
Montaigne remarked that there is more ado to interpret interpretations than to interpret things.
The rabbis had a saying for it: the Torah spoke in the language of men.
Jesus says: I am the bread of life; he that believeth on me shall never thirst.
Jesus speaks of a water that becomes, in the one who drinks it, a well springing up into everlasting life.
Paul says that we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God.
Jesus answers Pilate that his kingdom is not of this world, or his servants would fight.
Jesus says that the kingdom of God cometh not with observation, for the kingdom of God is within you.
Isaiah promised a child on whose shoulder the government shall be, called the Prince of Peace. How could those who waited for that child have known what kind of government was meant?
This is the promise the reading has in mind: the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David.
The letter to the Hebrews says that it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins.
The psalm says that the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit, a broken and a contrite heart.
Hosea has God say: I desired mercy, and not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.
Emerson says that every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
Jesus says that the tree is known by his fruit, and that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.
Samuel is told that man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart.
Isaiah's servant has no form nor comeliness, and no beauty that we should desire him.
The people of his own country ask: is not this the carpenter's son?
Jesus says: search the scriptures, for in them ye think ye have eternal life, and they testify of me.
The rabbis themselves taught that as a hammer breaks a stone into fragments, so from one verse emerge several explanations. Is it fair to say of such readers that they knew only the letter?
Philip asks a man reading Isaiah in his chariot: understandest thou what thou readest?
Carlyle, who admired Muhammad, called the Koran in translation as toilsome reading as he ever undertook. What does a reader need besides the page, and who is to blame when it is lacking?
Jesus asks his own disciples: having eyes, see ye not, and having ears, hear ye not?
Blake says of two readers of one Bible: thou read'st black where I read white.
Hume held that in matters of religion whatever is different is contrary, so that the religions cannot all be well founded. What would he need to be shown before granting that the books agree?
Jesus says that he is not come to destroy the law or the prophets, but to fulfil.
Asked why he speaks in parables, Jesus answers that to some it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom, and to others not.
The people round Jesus ask how long he will make them doubt: if thou be the Christ, tell us plainly. Is a hiddenness that sorts hearers fair to those who ask in earnest?
Peter's letter says of Paul's epistles that in them are some things hard to be understood.
Confucius said that if names be not correct, language is not in accordance with the truth of things.
In Rumi's story God says: I regard not the outside and the words, I regard the inside and the state of heart.
Juliet asks what is in a name: that which we call a rose by any other name would smell as sweet.
Plato's Socrates calls a name an instrument of teaching and of distinguishing natures. Can the ocean of meanings be reached without the river of names, or only by crossing it?
Emerson complained that churches are not built on Jesus's principles, but on his tropes.
Kabir has God say: I am neither in temple nor in mosque, neither in rites and ceremonies.
Sir Thomas Browne read nature as a universal and public manuscript that lies expansed unto the eyes of all.
Isaiah foresees a day when the ears of the deaf shall be unstopped.
Shakespeare's Iago says that he would as soon wear his heart upon his sleeve as let his outward action show it: I am not what I am.
Jesus compares hypocrites to whited sepulchres, beautiful outward, and within full of dead men's bones.
Jesus warns of those who come in sheep's clothing, but inwardly are ravening wolves.
The letter to the Hebrews says that no chastening for the present seemeth joyous, but afterward it yieldeth peaceable fruit.
Paul says that he is a Jew which is one inwardly, and circumcision is that of the heart, in the spirit.
Jesus says: cleanse first that which is within the cup, that the outside may be clean also.
Hamlet says that his mourning clothes are but the trappings of woe: he has that within which passeth show.
Shelley says of high poetry that veil after veil may be undrawn, and the inmost beauty of the meaning never exposed.
Jesus says of tithes and of judgment, mercy and faith: these ought ye to have done, and not to leave the other undone.
The psalmist says to God: in thy light shall we see light.
Aquinas held that since the author of scripture is God, it is not unfitting that one word of it should have several senses.
The psalmist announces: I will open my mouth in a parable, I will utter dark sayings of old.
Naaman was wroth at being told simply to wash, having thought the prophet would come out and strike his hand over the place.

galatians-which-things-are-an-allegory.text: For it is written, that Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman. But he who was of the bondwoman was born after the flesh; but he of the freewoman was by promise. Which things are an allegory: for these are the two covenants; the one from the mount Sinai, which gendereth to bondage, which is Agar. For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia, and answereth to Jerusalem which now is, and is in bondage with her children. But Jerusalem which is above is free, which is the mother of us all

john-son-of-man-which-is-in-heaven.text: If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things? And no man hath ascended up to heaven, but he that came down from heaven, even the Son of man which is in heaven

psalm-open-my-mouth-in-a-parable.text: Give ear, O my people, to my law: incline your ears to the words of my mouth. I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old: Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us

corinthians-all-drank-of-that-spiritual-.text: Moreover, brethren, I would not that ye should be ignorant, how that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea; And were all baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea; And did all eat the same spiritual meat; And did all drink the same spiritual drink: for they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them: and that Rock was Christ

luke-throne-of-his-father-david.text: He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest: and the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David: And he shall reign over the house of Jacob for ever; and of his kingdom there shall be no end

hebrews-blood-of-bulls-and-goats.text: For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me: In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure
